metadata.title: Romanesque Capital Fragment: Daniel in the Lions' Den
metadata.medium: Carved Granitic Stone with traces of polychromy

exhibitionConstraints.artistAutonomyBoundary: Preserve spiritual gravitas. Virtual reconstructions of missing stone chunks must remain visually translucent to avoid confusing visitors about what is authentic stone vs. hypothetical restoration.

chapters.narrativeText: Notice the deep incisions made by hand chisels into coarse-grain northern granite, surviving eight centuries of outdoor weathering.

hotspots.title: Microscopic Lapis Lazuli Pigment
hotspots.description: Multi-spectral macro imaging reveals microscopic lapis lazuli and vermilion pigment traces in the lion's mane folds.

chapters.narrativeText: Hypothetical reconstruction of the medieval stone carver's guild: chisel angles, geometric compass ratios, and theological iconography.

hotspots.title: Toothed Claw Chisel Toolmarks
hotspots.description: 3D photogrammetric normal map highlighting tool strokes unique to the 12th-century atelier.

chapters.narrativeText: The capital originally supported the north portal archway of the monastic abbey, destroyed during the 1755 earthquake.

hotspots.title: Volumetric Arch Re-contextualization
hotspots.description: Semireflective holographic ghost of the entire portal archway hovering above the pedestal.

quickSurveyQuestions: Did seeing the translucent architectural reconstruction help you understand the original church setting?
Was the spatial holographic display intuitive and non-distracting?
Did you feel the distinction between genuine stone and hypothetical reconstruction was clear?
